q: What does the term "Silk Routes" primarily refer to?
o: Routes used exclusively inside Europe for gold trade
Vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links connecting Asia with Europe and northern Africa
Railway lines built across Siberia in 1900
Only sea routes connecting India and Australia
e: The Silk Routes are a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world, connecting vast regions of Asia with Europe and northern Africa by land and sea.

q: In which country did the devastating Potato Famine occur during 1845–1849?
o: England
Ireland
Spain
America
e: Europe's poor peasants became so dependent on potatoes that when disease destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s (1845–1849), hundreds of thousands died of starvation in Ireland.

q: When did the Great Economic Depression begin?
e: The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s, causing catastrophic declines in production, employment, incomes and trade across most parts of the world.

q: In the 1890s, the fast-spreading cattle disease called "Rinderpest" devastated which continent?
o: Europe
Africa
North America
Australia
e: In Africa, in the 1890s, a fast-spreading disease of cattle plague or rinderpest had a terrifying impact on people's livelihoods and the local economy, killing 90% of the cattle.

q: Which of the following institutions are famously known as the "Bretton Woods twins"?
o: WTO and UNESCO
International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (IBRD)
UN Security Council and WHO
UNICEF and ILO
e: The IMF and the World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development) were established at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference and are referred to as the Bretton Woods twins.

q: In which year was the Bretton Woods Conference held in New Hampshire, USA?
e: The Bretton Woods framework was agreed upon at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference held in July 1944 at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA.

q: Who were "Girmitiya" (indentured) labourers?
o: Bonded labourers hired under a contract to work for an employer for a specific period of time in order to pay off their passage to a new country
British landlords in Punjab Canal Colonies
European bankers in London
Textile factory owners in Bombay
e: Indentured labour was a bonded labourer under contract to work for an employer for a specific amount of time (usually five years) to pay off his passage to a new country or home.

q: In which year was the system of indentured labour migration officially abolished in India?
e: Following strong opposition from Indian nationalist leaders who described it as abusive and cruel, the system of indentured labour migration was abolished in 1921.

q: Which deadly germ helped Spanish conquerors decimate the native populations of America in the 16th century?
o: Rinderpest
Smallpox
Cholera
Malaria
e: The most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors was not a conventional military weapon; it was the germs such as those of smallpox that they carried on their person against which native Americans had no immunity.

q: What were the "Corn Laws" in Britain?
o: Laws encouraging free import of cheap American wheat
Laws allowing the British government to restrict the import of corn under pressure from landed groups
Laws banning potato cultivation in Ireland
Laws regulating railway speeds
e: Under pressure from landed groups, the British government restricted the import of corn; the laws allowing the government to do this were commonly known as the "Corn Laws".

q: Who was the well-known pioneer of mass production in the automobile industry using the assembly line?
o: James Watt
Henry Ford
John Maynard Keynes
Richard Arkwright
e: Car manufacturer Henry Ford was a well-known pioneer of mass production in the 1920s, adapting the conveyor-belt assembly line to his Detroit car plant.

q: Which model was the world's first mass-produced car built by Henry Ford?
o: Model A
T-Model Ford
Ford Mustang
Model S
e: The T-Model Ford was the world's first mass-produced car, rolling off Henry Ford's assembly line at three-minute intervals.

q: Which countries were part of the "Allies" during World War I?
o: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey
Britain, France and Russia (later joined by the US)
Japan, Italy and Germany
Spain, Portugal and Switzerland
e: The First World War was fought between two power blocs: the Allies (Britain, France and Russia, later joined by the US) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey).

q: Which countries constituted the "Axis Powers" during the Second World War (1939–1945)?
o: Britain, France and the US
Nazi Germany, Japan and Italy
Russia, China and India
Austria, Belgium and Holland
e: The Second World War was fought between the Axis powers (mainly Nazi Germany, Japan and Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the US).

q: What did "Cowries" (कौड़ियाँ) serve as in pre-modern long-distance trade for more than a millennium?
o: Decorative weapons
Currency (मुद्रा)
Agricultural tools
Ship anchors
e: For more than a millennia, cowries (the Hindi cowdi or seashells, used as a form of currency) from the Maldives found their way to China and East Africa.

q: What is "El Dorado" often referred to as in 16th-century European legends?
o: A deadly plague
The fabled city of gold in South America
A British shipping company
A Chinese silk market
e: In the 17th century, European legends spread about South America's fabled wealth, prompting many expeditions in search of El Dorado, the fabled city of gold.

q: What is "NIEO" demanded by the Group of 77 (G-77) developing countries?
o: National Industrial Employment Organisation
New International Economic Order
North Indian Export Office
New Imperial Economic Organisation
e: Most developing countries did not benefit from the fast growth of Western economies in the 1950s–60s, so they organised as G-77 to demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO).

q: Which Nobel Prize-winning writer is descended from indentured labour migrants from India?
o: Rabindranath Tagore
V. S. Naipaul
Ruskin Bond
Salman Rushdie
e: Nobel Prize-winning writer V. S. Naipaul, along with West Indies cricketers Shivnarine Chanderpaul and Ramnaresh Sarwan, are descendants of indentured labour migrants from India.

q: Which region of Punjab was transformed by building a network of irrigation canals to grow wheat and cotton for export during British rule?
o: Canal Colonies (नहर बस्तियाँ)
Tarai Marshes
Rann of Kutch
Gudem Hills
e: In west Punjab, the British Indian government built a network of irrigation canals to transform semi-desert wastes into fertile agricultural lands; the areas irrigated by the new canals were called Canal Colonies.

q: Which annual Muslim festival in Trinidad transformed into a riotous carnival called "Hosay" joined by workers of all races and religions?
o: Eid-ul-Fitr
Muharram procession
Diwali
Christmas
e: In Trinidad the annual Muharram procession was transformed into a riotous carnival called "Hosay" (for Imam Hussain) in which workers of all races and religions joined.

q: Which crops did NOT exist in Europe or Asia until about five centuries ago, after Christopher Columbus reached the Americas?
o: Rice, wheat and barley
Potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes
Tea, cotton and indigo
Pepper and cinnamon
e: Many common foods such as potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes were unknown to our ancestors until about five centuries ago and were introduced to Europe and Asia after Columbus reached the Americas.

q: What is the full form of IMF, established at the Bretton Woods Conference?
o: Indian Monetary Federation
International Monetary Fund
Internal Market Finance
International Manufacturing Forum
e: The Bretton Woods Conference established the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to deal with external surpluses and deficits of its member nations.

q: In which city did the European powers meet in 1885 to carve up Africa among themselves?
o: London
Paris
Berlin
Vienna
e: In 1885 the big European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa between them, drawing borders across Africa using straight lines on a map.

q: Which region of China saw Buddhism emerge from eastern India and spread along the Silk Routes?
o: Judaism
Buddhism
Zoroastrianism
Sikhism
e: Buddhism emerged from eastern India and spread in several directions through intersecting points on the silk routes, alongside Christian missionaries and Muslim preachers.

q: When did the Bretton Woods institutions (IMF and World Bank) commence their financial operations?
e: Although agreed upon at the Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944, the IMF and the World Bank commenced financial operations in 1947.

q: What does "Tariff" (आयात शुल्क) mean according to NCERT?
o: A fixed wage paid to factory workers
A tax imposed on a country's imports from the rest of the world, levied at the point of entry
An export subsidy given to farmers
A loan from the IMF
e: A tariff is a tax imposed on a country's imports from the rest of the world; tariffs are levied at the point of entry, i.e., at the border or the airport.

q: What is "Chutney music", popular in Trinidad and Guyana, an example of?
o: Pure European classical opera
Cultural fusion resulting from post-indenture Indian and global cultural mixing
Ancient African royal hymns
American jazz of the 1950s
e: "Chutney music", popular in Trinidad and Guyana, is a creative contemporary expression of the post-indenture experience and cultural fusion.

q: In India, most indentured workers came from which regions during the 19th century?
o: Punjab and Gujarat
Present-day eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu
Assam and Nagaland
Kerala and Goa
e: In the 19th century, hundreds of thousands of Indian labourers went to work on plantations and mines worldwide; most came from eastern UP, Bihar, central India and dry districts of Tamil Nadu.

q: Which two Indian banking/trading groups financed export agriculture in Central and Southeast Asia using either their own funds or funds borrowed from European banks?
o: Tata and Birla
Shikaripuri shroffs and Nattukottai Chettiars
British East India Company and Dutch VOC
Marwaris of Assam and Patidars of Gujarat
e: Shikaripuri shroffs and Nattukottai Chettiars were amongst the many groups of Indian bankers and traders who financed export agriculture in Central and Southeast Asia with sophisticated money-transfer systems.

q: Which US-based institution holds effective right of veto over key IMF and World Bank decisions?
o: United Kingdom
United States of America (US)
Russia
Japan
e: Decision-making in the Bretton Woods institutions is controlled by Western industrial powers, and the US has an effective right of veto over key IMF and World Bank decisions.

q: In the Bretton Woods system, national currencies were pegged to which currency at a fixed exchange rate?
o: British Pound Sterling
US Dollar (pegged to gold at $35 per ounce)
Japanese Yen
Indian Rupee
e: The Bretton Woods system was based on fixed exchange rates: national currencies (e.g. Indian rupee) were pegged to the US dollar, while the dollar itself was anchored to gold at a fixed price of $35 per ounce.

q: Which invention of the 1870s enabled slaughtered meat from America, Australia or New Zealand to be shipped cheaply to Europe?
o: Telegraph lines
Refrigerated ships
Internal combustion planes
Nuclear submarines
e: Before the 1870s, live animals were shipped from America to Europe, taking up lot of space and falling sick/dying on the voyage. Refrigerated ships allowed animals to be slaughtered at the starting point and transported as frozen meat.

q: By what percentage did the share of Indian cotton textile exports decline between around 1800 and the 1870s?
o: From 30% to under 3%
From 80% to 50%
From 10% to 8%
It rose from 5% to 35%
e: With British tariffs and cheap Lancashire mill imports, the share of cotton textiles in Indian exports declined from some 30% around 1800 to 15% by 1815, and by the 1870s had dropped to below 3%.

q: Between 1812 and 1871, what happened to the share of RAW COTTON exports from India?
o: Fell from 30% to 3%
Rose from 5% to 35%
Remained fixed at 10%
Stopped completely
e: While exports of Indian cotton manufactures fell, exports of raw materials increased equally fast: between 1812 and 1871, the share of raw cotton exports rose from 5% to 35%.

q: Which crop grown in India was exported in large quantities by the British to China to finance British tea and other imports from China?
o: Jute
Opium (अफीम)
Coffee
Sugarcane
e: From the 1820s, British shipments of opium to China grew rapidly and became for a while India's single largest export, using the returns to finance British tea and other imports from China.

q: Who observed during the 1930s Great Depression that Indian gold exports promoted global economic recovery and helped Britain in particular?
o: Adam Smith
John Maynard Keynes
Friedrich List
Amartya Sen
e: Because colonial India refused to reduce revenue demands during the Great Depression, indebted peasants sold jewellery and India exported precious metals (gold); famous economist John Maynard Keynes thought Indian gold exports promoted global economic recovery.

q: In 1890s Africa, who introduced Rinderpest (cattle plague) to East Africa?
o: Through infected cattle imported from British Asia to feed Italian soldiers invading Eritrea in East Africa
Through ships arriving from Brazil
Through migrating European sheep
Through African coffee traders
e: Rinderpest arrived in Africa in the late 1880s, carried by infected cattle imported from British Asia to feed the Italian soldiers invading Eritrea in East Africa.

q: Approximately what percentage of Africa's cattle was killed by Rinderpest on its destructive path from east to west?
e: Along its way from East Africa to the Atlantic coast (1892) and the Cape (five years later), rinderpest killed 90 per cent of the cattle, destroying African livelihoods.

q: What was "Rastafarianism", made famous by Jamaican reggae star Bob Marley?
o: A European banking law
A protest religion reflecting social and cultural links with Indian migrants in the Caribbean
A farming technique in Fiji
A Chinese porcelain trade guild
e: The protest religion of Rastafarianism (made famous by Jamaican reggae star Bob Marley) is also said to reflect social and cultural links with Indian migrants to the Caribbean.

q: Which two groups of European/American powers gained territories during the late 19th-century Scramble for Africa and colonial expansion?
o: Belgium and Germany became new colonial powers, and the US also became a colonial power in the late 1890s by taking over some colonies earlier held by Spain
India and China colonised Africa
Switzerland and Norway divided Australia
Italy colonised North America
e: While Britain and France made vast additions to overseas territories, Belgium and Germany became new colonial powers, and the US took over some Spanish colonies in the late 1890s.

q: Why was World War I called the "first modern industrial war"?
o: It saw the use of machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons on a massive scale—all increasingly products of modern large-scale industry
It was fought entirely by robots
Only one factory was damaged
It lasted only two weeks
e: WWI involved the world's leading industrial nations and harnessed modern industry to inflict the greatest possible destruction using machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons, killing 9 million and injuring 20 million.

q: Which economic status did the United States acquire at the end of World War I?
o: It transformed from being an international debtor to an international creditor
It went completely bankrupt and borrowed from Britain
It closed all banks in Wall Street
It reverted to the barter system
e: During WWI, Britain borrowed large sums of money from US banks and the US public; thus the war transformed the US from being an international debtor to an international creditor (with Americans owning more overseas assets than foreign governments/citizens owned in the US).

q: By how much did wheat prices fall in India between 1928 and 1934 during the Great Depression?
o: 50% (halved)
e: India's exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934; as international prices crashed, wheat prices in India fell by 50 per cent.

q: Which Indian agricultural commodity produced in Bengal saw raw prices crash by more than 60% during the Great Depression?
o: Wheat
Raw Jute
Tea
Coffee
e: Peasants of Bengal who grew raw jute for processing in factories for export in the form of gunny bags saw gunny exports collapse and the price of raw jute crash more than 60 per cent.

q: What does "Fixed Exchange Rates" vs "Floating Exchange Rates" mean in international trade?
o: Fixed rates stay linked by government intervention to prevent movement, while floating rates fluctuate depending on demand and supply in foreign exchange markets
Fixed rates change every hour automatically
Floating rates are allowed only on ships
Both mean using silver coins only
e: When exchange rates are fixed, governments intervene to prevent movements in them; flexible or floating exchange rates fluctuate depending on demand and supply of currencies in foreign exchange markets.

q: Who was sent by the New York Herald to find Dr David Livingstone, a missionary and explorer in Africa?
o: Christopher Columbus
Sir Henry Morton Stanley
Marco Polo
Vasco da Gama
e: Sir Henry Morton Stanley was a journalist and explorer sent by the New York Herald to find Livingstone; Stanley's explorations helped Europeans map and conquer Africa.

q: Roughly how many people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century?
o: 5 million
50 million (5 crore)
500 million
1 million
e: Nearly 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century, and all over the world some 150 million are estimated to have left their homes in search of a better future.

q: Which three "flows" or movements were identified by economists within 19th-century international economic exchanges?
o: Trade (goods), Labour (migration of people), and Capital (investments)
Electricity, Oil, and Internet
Only rivers, oceans, and winds
Artillery, Railways, and Telegraphs
e: Economists identify three types of movement or "flows" within international economic exchanges: the flow of trade (in goods like cloth or wheat), the flow of labour (migration), and the movement of capital.

q: What was Britain's "Trade Surplus" with India in the 19th century used to settle?
o: To balance Britain's trade deficits with other countries and pay "home charges"
To build free universities in every Indian village
To pay Indian weavers higher wages
To buy gold exclusively for Indian peasants
e: Britain had a multilateral settlement system where its trade surplus with India helped balance its trade deficits with other countries and pay the so-called "home charges" (remittances, pensions, external debt interest).

q: Where did Henry Ford get the inspiration for the assembly line method used in his Detroit car plant?
o: From a British textile mill in Manchester
From the assembly line of a Chicago slaughterhouse
From a French vineyard
From a Calcutta jute mill
e: Henry Ford adapted the assembly line of a Chicago slaughterhouse (in which slaughtered animals were picked apart by butchers as they came down a conveyor belt) to his new car plant in Detroit.

q: What was the daily wage Henry Ford offered in January 1914 to stop workers from quitting the exhausting assembly line?
o: $1 per day
$5 per day (doubling the daily wage)
$25 per day
$0.50 per day
e: Unable to cope with the stress of working on assembly lines, workers quit in large numbers; in desperation Ford doubled the daily wage to $5 in January 1914 while simultaneously banning trade unions in his plants.

q: Which country had been isolated from the world economy since its 1949 revolution before re-entering global manufacturing and becoming an attractive destination for MNC investment from the late 1970s?
o: Japan
China
Brazil
Egypt
e: China had been cut off from the post-war world economy since its revolution in 1949, but new economic policies and the collapse of the Soviet Union brought many countries back into the world economy; low wages in China attracted MNCs.

q: From which century did China restrict overseas contacts and retreat into isolation, allowing Europe to gradually emerge as the centre of world trade?
o: 10th century
15th century
19th century
20th century
e: Until well into the 18th century, China and India were among the world's richest countries; however, from the 15th century China is said to have restricted overseas contacts and retreated into isolation, while the Americas rose in importance.

q: Why was the post-World War II Bretton Woods system able to maintain unprecedented stability and growth for Western industrial nations from 1950 to 1970?
o: World trade grew annually at over 8% and incomes at nearly 5%, with unemployment averaging less than 5% in most industrial countries
Because all Asian countries were banned from trading
Because currencies fluctuated wildly every day
Because only gold coins were used in stores
e: The Bretton Woods system inaugurated an era of unprecedented growth of trade and incomes for Western industrial nations and Japan: world trade grew annually at over 8% between 1950 and 1970 and incomes at nearly 5%, with stable growth and <5% unemployment.

q: Why did the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates eventually collapse in the 1960s–70s?
o: The rising costs of US overseas involvements weakened the US's finances and competitive strength, so the US dollar could no longer maintain its value in relation to gold
Britain bought all US gold reserves
India abolished the Reserve Bank
Japan banned the US dollar in 1950
e: From the 1960s, rising costs of US overseas involvements weakened US finances; the US dollar could no longer command confidence as the principal currency or maintain its fixed value to gold, leading to collapse of fixed exchange rates and introduction of floating exchange rates.

q: What happened during World War I when able-bodied European men went to fight in the trenches?
o: Industries were restructured to produce war-related goods and women stepped in to undertake jobs earlier considered only men's jobs
All European factories remained empty with zero output
Millions of Indian peasants moved to Paris factories
Women were prohibited from leaving homes
e: Because most of the killed and maimed in WWI were men of working age, household incomes declined and women stepped in to undertake jobs that earlier only men were expected to do.

q: Which Indian city/region did Hyderabadi Sindhi traders venture beyond to establish thriving emporia at busy ports worldwide?
o: Hyderabadi Sindhi traders
Chotanagpur miners
Bengal indigo ryots
Madras fishermen
e: Hyderabadi Sindhi traders ventured beyond European colonies and from the 1860s established flourishing emporia at busy ports worldwide, selling local and imported curios to tourists.

q: What was "G-77" formed in response to during the post-World War II decades?
o: Because most developing countries did not benefit from the fast growth of Western economies and remained under former colonial powers' influence at IMF/World Bank, so they demanded a New International Economic Order (NIEO)
To build nuclear weapons together
To abolish the United Nations
To join the Axis Powers
e: In the 1950s–60s, newly independent developing countries saw IMF and World Bank still dominated by former colonial powers, so they organised as G-77 demanding NIEO for real control over natural resources, fairer raw material prices and market access.

q: During the inter-war agricultural crisis after WWI, which regions saw wheat production drop sharply while Canada, America and Australia expanded dramatically?
o: Eastern Europe; when Eastern European output revived after the war, it created a glut in wheat output, grain prices fell, rural incomes declined and farmers fell deeper into debt
South America; output never recovered
Japan; rice replaced wheat everywhere
Australia; production stopped after 1918
e: Eastern Europe had been a major supplier of wheat before WWI; when its supplies disrupted during the war, wheat production expanded in Canada, America and Australia, leading to post-war overproduction and collapsing prices.

q: How did the 1929 Great Depression begin and hit countries outside the United States?
o: US overseas lenders panicked at the first sign of trouble in 1928 and withdrew loans, causing acute crisis in Europe (failure of major banks, collapse of currencies like the British pound) and slump in Latin America/Asia
Because Britain refused to buy tea from India
Because Rinderpest reached New York
Because Henry Ford stopped selling cars in 1920
e: In the mid-1920s many countries financed investments through US loans; when US overseas lending panicked and fell sharply from over $1 billion in early 1928 to a quarter of that within a year, countries dependent on US loans faced acute crisis.

q: Why did the abolition of the Corn Laws in Britain lead to global economic transformation rather than starvation in Britain?
o: Food could be imported into Britain more cheaply than it could be produced within the country; British agriculture failed to compete, vast lands lay uncultivated, workers migrated to cities/overseas, and lands around the world (Eastern Europe, Russia, America, Australia) were cleared to feed Britain
Britain stopped eating bread completely
British peasants bought all farms in Canada immediately
Prices in London increased tenfold
e: As food prices fell, consumption in Britain rose; faster industrial growth led to higher incomes and more food imports, driving railway, harbour and agricultural expansion across Eastern Europe, Russia, America and Australia.

q: How did the British colonial authorities and employers force Africans to work for wages in plantations and mines after Rinderpest?
o: Colonial governments, planters and mine owners monopolised the scarce cattle resources left after Rinderpest, alongside earlier heavy taxes and inheritance laws that displaced peasants
They offered equal shares of diamond mines to every African worker
They banned European immigration
They lowered taxes to zero
e: Historically Africa had abundant land and scarce population, so Africans had little reason to work for wages; Rinderpest destroyed 90% of cattle, and control over remaining cattle enabled Europeans to conquer Africa and force Africans into the labour market.

q: Why was 19th-century indentured labour migration described by historians and nationalists as a "new system of slavery"?
o: Agents often provided false information about destinations, modes of travel and living conditions, sometimes forcibly abducted migrants, and on arrival labourers found harsh working conditions and few legal rights
Workers were paid millions of gold coins upfront
Contract duration was only one week
Only European aristocrats were recruited as indentured labour
e: Workers recruited by agents often had no idea of long sea voyages or harsh plantation conditions; on arrival they faced brutal living and working conditions with virtually no legal rights.

q: Why did many Indian indentured workers choose to stay on in Caribbean islands, Fiji or Mauritius even after their five-year contract ended?
o: Poverty and caste oppression back home in India, plus the desire to start a new life after having built community networks abroad
Because ships to India were banned forever
Because Britain outlawed farming in Uttar Pradesh
Because India refused to allow any migrant back
e: Many stayed on after their contracts ended, or returned to India only briefly before going back, blending Indian traditions with local cultures and creating new hybrid communities.

q:
Arrange the following global historical events in chronological order:
I. Abolition of indentured labour
II. Berlin Conference partitioning Africa
III. Bretton Woods Conference
IV. Start of the Great Depression
o: II → I → IV → III
I → II → IV → III
II → IV → I → III
III → IV → I → II
e: Berlin Conference (1885) → Abolition of indentured labour (1921) → Start of the Great Depression (1929) → Bretton Woods Conference (1944).

q: Why were European powers NOT forced to kill native Americans predominantly by gunfire in the 16th century?
o: Because native Americans had been isolated from the rest of the world for millions of years and lacked immunity against European diseases like smallpox, which spread ahead of European troops
Because Native Americans voluntarily invited Spain to rule them
Because gunpowder failed to work in tropical climates
Because no native populations lived in South America
e: Guns could be bought or captured and turned against the invaders, but not diseases like smallpox to which the conquerors were mostly immune while native Americans succumbed rapidly.

q: Which key economic difference distinguished the "Hire Purchase" system in 1920s USA and why did it worsen the 1929 crash?
o: Consumers bought houses, cars and appliances on weekly/monthly credit instalments fueled by booming wages; when employment fell in 1929, households could not repay loans and had to give up homes and goods, collapsing banks
Workers only bought goods using gold bullion
Hire purchase applied strictly to agricultural land in Europe
The US government forbade consumer loans in 1925
e: The housing and consumer boom of the 1920s created the basis of US prosperity via credit-driven "hire purchase"; when the 1929 depression struck, families trapped in debt defaulted, bankrupting banks and deepening the slump.

q: What role did "technology" play in lowering food prices and improving European living standards in the late 19th century?
o: Faster railways, lighter wagons, larger ships and refrigerated ships lowered transport costs so frozen meat, wheat and butter became affordable for the European poor
Factories stopped producing textiles and grew wheat indoors
Airplanes delivered fresh milk daily across the Atlantic in 1880
Electric tractors were used globally in 1850
e: NCERT explains that technological advances (railways, steamships, telegraph, refrigerated ships) were often the result of larger social, political and economic factors—and refrigerated ships turned meat from an expensive luxury into everyday food for the European poor, promoting social peace at home.

q: Why was urban India relatively less severely affected by the Great Depression (1929–34) compared to rural agricultural peasants?
o: Because prices fell sharply, town-dwelling landowners who received fixed rents and middle-class salaried employees found everything cost less, while peasants saw crop incomes collapse while colonial revenue stayed high
Because urban Indians exported 100% of industrial steel
Because cities paid zero taxes
Because urban wages tripled during the Depression
e: Because of falling prices, those with fixed incomes — like town-dwelling landowners who received rents and middle-class salaried employees — found themselves better off, whereas peasants producing for the world market were worst hit.

q: How did Indian nationalist leaders use the Great Depression in 1931 to mobilise rural support for the Civil Disobedience Movement?
o: Colonial refusal to reduce revenue demands despite falling agricultural prices pushed peasants into selling savings, land and jewellery, fuelling Gandhi's Civil Disobedience Movement in 1931
They thanked the British for raising rural incomes
They urged farmers to burn all gold coins
They supported higher jute export taxes
e: In 1931, the depression was immediately felt across rural India, and despite peasants plunging into debt and distress-selling precious metals, the colonial government refused to reduce revenue demands—driving rural unrest behind Gandhiji's CDM.

q:
Match the following historical concepts/terms with their correct context:
(i) Canal Colonies (ii) Hosay (iii) Rinderpest (iv) Bretton Woods twins
o: (i)-West Punjab irrigation, (ii)-Trinidad carnival, (iii)-African cattle plague, (iv)-IMF & World Bank
(i)-Trinidad carnival, (ii)-IMF & World Bank, (iii)-West Punjab irrigation, (iv)-African cattle plague
(i)-African cattle plague, (ii)-West Punjab irrigation, (iii)-Trinidad carnival, (iv)-IMF & World Bank
(i)-IMF & World Bank, (ii)-African cattle plague, (iii)-Trinidad carnival, (iv)-West Punjab irrigation
e: Canal Colonies = West Punjab irrigation settlements; Hosay = Muharram carnival in Trinidad; Rinderpest = cattle plague in 1890s Africa; Bretton Woods twins = IMF & World Bank.

q: What dual lesson did economists and politicians draw from the inter-war economic experience (1919–1939) when designing the post-WWII Bretton Woods system?
o: (1) An industrial society based on mass production cannot be sustained without mass consumption (requiring high and stable incomes/employment); (2) Full employment can only be guaranteed through government intervention and control over flows of goods, capital and labour
Only that tariffs should be 100% forever
Only that governments must never regulate banks
Only that gold mining should replace agriculture
e: Economists and politicians drew two key lessons from inter-war chaos: first, mass production requires mass consumption backed by stable employment and incomes (via government intervention); second, external economic links must be controlled by governments to achieve full employment.

q: Why did US and European industrial production and jobs move increasingly to Asian countries like India, China and Brazil from the late 1970s?
o: Relocating operations to low-wage countries boosted corporate profits in a world of rising Asian competitiveness and collapsing fixed exchange rates
Because electricity stopped working in New York
Because the World Bank forced US factories to close in 1975
Because China had the highest labour wages in the world
e: MNCs began shifting production operations to low-wage Asian countries in the late 1970s because wages were relatively low in countries like China, enabling them to capture world markets at lower cost.

q: How did the Great Depression affect India's industrial investment in the early 1930s compared to peasants?
o: Industrial investment in urban India actually grew as the colonial government extended tariff protection to certain Indian industries under nationalist pressure
Every cotton and steel mill in Bombay and Jamshedpur closed forever
Foreign cloth imports tripled during 1931–34
Indian cities lost 50% of their railway tracks

All 1, 2 and 3
e: Statement 2 is incorrect: in India, colonial authorities REFUSED to reduce revenue demands even as prices halved, pushing peasants into debt and gold distress sales. Statements 1 and 3 match exact NCERT figures (over 4,000 banks closed by 1933; 110,000 companies collapsed by 1932).

q: Why was Henry Ford's Detroit assembly line initially resisted by workers, and what trade-off did Ford impose when doubling wages to $5/day in 1914?
o: Workers could not control the pace of work or take a break and quit in large numbers; when doubling pay to $5/day, Ford banned trade unions from operating in his plants and recovered the wage hike by speeding up the production line even further
Workers objected because cars were painted black only
Ford closed the conveyor belt in 1915
Ford allowed trade unions to run the board of directors
e: On the assembly line, workers could neither pause nor delay motions or even have a friendly word with workmates; when Ford doubled wages in Jan 1914, he simultaneously banned trade unions and later called it "the best cost-cutting decision" because he repeatedly sped up the conveyor belt.

q: How did the Great Depression expose the fragility of the post-WWI US economic boom of the 1920s?
o: The consumer boom in houses and appliances relied heavily on easy bank credit ("hire purchase") and speculative stock investment; once agricultural crisis and loan withdrawals began, unemployment prevented repayments, bankrupting thousands of banks and destroying household savings
US industry had zero mass production before 1930
The US had no banks in 1929
All US workers worked on collective farms
e: With falling incomes and vanishing jobs, US households could not repay debts incurred during the 1920s credit-fuelled consumer boom; businesses closed, banks went bankrupt (over 4,000 by 1933) and the US banking system collapsed.

q: What does NCERT mean by "a new system of slavery" when describing indentured labour, and yet how did labourers find ways to survive culturally?
o: Some ran away into the wilds; others developed new forms of individual and collective self-expression by blending different cultural forms—such as Hosay in Trinidad, Rastafarianism, and Chutney music
They immediately bought steamships back to India in week one
They refused to celebrate any festivals or play music
They replaced English with Sanskrit in all British courts
e: Despite harsh conditions, indentured workers discovered survival mechanisms: escaping into the wilds or blending old and new cultures into vibrant hybrid traditions like Hosay, Rastafarianism and Chutney music.

q: Which pair of statements accurately compares India's 18th-century vs 19th-century position in the world economy?
o: Until 18th century: India & China were among the world's richest nations exporting fine textiles globally; By 19th century: British industrialisation & tariffs reduced India's textile exports to <3% while turning India into a supplier of raw cotton, opium and indigo and a captive market for British manufactures
Until 18th century: India imported all textiles from Manchester; By 19th century: India dominated European machine tool exports
Until 18th century: India had no overseas trade; By 19th century: China colonised India
In both centuries, India remained completely isolated from global trade
e: This directly traces India's transformation from being one of the world's pre-eminent textile suppliers in the 18th century into a raw-material exporter and captive British market in the 19th century.

q: Why did the "Great Depression" hit export-oriented economies like Japan, Germany, Australia and India differently from the USSR?
o: Because the USSR was insulated from global capitalist markets through state-planned industrialisation, whereas market-linked countries depended heavily on international trade prices and US loans
Because USSR used gold cowries from Maldives
Because the USSR was the richest stock market in New York
Because India funded the USSR during 1930
e: Unlike capitalist market economies linked by US loans and global commodity prices, the Soviet Union remained insulated from the Great Depression's crash through its state-controlled planned economy.

q: Which economic demand was central to the Group of 77 (G-77) call for a "New International Economic Order (NIEO)"?
o: Real control over their natural resources, more development assistance, fairer prices for raw materials, and better access for their manufactured goods in developed countries' markets
Elimination of all developing-country exports
Transferring US veto power to Britain alone
Returning to 19th-century Corn Laws
e: By NIEO, G-77 meant a system that would give them real control over their natural resources, more development assistance, fairer prices for raw materials, and better access for their manufactured goods in developed countries' markets.

q: What happened during World War II that severely affected Europe and Asia both economically and demographically?
o: At least 60 million people (about 3% of the 1939 world population) are believed to have been killed, many millions more injured, more civilians died than soldiers, and vast parts of Europe and Asia were devastated, leaving the US and the USSR as dominant powers
Only 1 million soldiers died with zero civilian casualties
Europe became wealthier than the US in 1945
Bombardment damaged only rural farms, sparing all cities
e: NCERT notes WWII caused immense devastation: at least 60 million dead (~3% of 1939 world population), many more civilians than soldiers killed, cities destroyed by aerial bombardment, and two crucial post-war influences—US emergence as economic/political/military giant in the Western world and Soviet dominance.

q: Why does NCERT cite the example of Indian entrepreneurs like Shikaripuri shroffs, Nattukottai Chettiars and Hyderabadi Sindhi traders alongside colonial British trade?
o: To show that even under colonial rule, Indian bankers and traders actively participated in global finance, developed indigenous corporate organisations and ran global trade networks across Asia and port cities worldwide
To claim Indian bankers ruled London
To prove all Indian traders worked as British soldiers
Because they invented the T-Model Ford
e: Indian traders and moneylenders followed European colonisers into Africa, financed export agriculture in Central and Southeast Asia, operated indigenous systems to transfer money over large distances, and opened global emporia.

q: What was "The Age of Discovery" / 16th-century shrinking of the pre-modern world driven by?
o: European sailors found a sea route to Asia and successfully crossed the western ocean to America, transforming the Indian Ocean into a bustling hub connected directly with American wealth and European trade
Completion of the Panama Canal in 1500
Invention of railways in South America in 1510
Opening of Bretton Woods in 1550
e: The pre-modern world shrank greatly in the 16th century after European sailors found a sea route to Asia and also crossed the western ocean to America, linking the hitherto isolated Americas and Asia-Europe circuits.

q: Why was the post-World War I recovery especially difficult for Britain compared to India and Japan?
o: While Britain was preoccupied with war, industries had developed in India and Japan; after the war Britain found it difficult to recapture its earlier dominant position in the Indian market and to compete with Japan internationally, and was also burdened with huge external debts to the US
Because Britain lost all its railways during trench warfare inside London
Because India conquered Japan in 1920
Because the US stopped using ships after 1918
e: Britain, which was the world's leading economy in the pre-war period, faced a prolonged crisis after WWI because industries developed in India and Japan during the war, making it hard for Britain to recapture Indian markets or compete with Japan while owing massive war debts to the US.

q: Which statement accurately describes Britain's post-war unemployment crisis in the early 1920s?
o: When the war boom ended, production contracted and unemployment increased; in 1921 one in every five British workers was out of work
Every British soldier immediately received a high-paying car factory job in 1921
Britain had 0% unemployment throughout the 1920s
All British agricultural exports doubled in 1921
e: When the war boom ended in Britain, production contracted and unemployment increased while government reduced bloated war expenditures; in 1921 one in every five British workers was out of work, creating immense anxiety and uncertainty.

q: What did the "three flows" of 19th-century world economy highlight about national borders and sovereignty vs capital mobility?
o: Although all three flows were closely interwoven and affected people's lives deeply, labour migration was often more restricted than the flows of goods or capital
Only labour moved freely while goods never crossed oceans
Neither goods nor capital moved in the 19th century
Only passports from India were valid globally
e: NCERT notes that all three flows were closely interwoven and affected peoples' lives more deeply than ever before; the interconnections could sometimes be broken—for example, labour migration was often more restricted than goods or capital flows.

q: Identify the INCORRECT match between destination countries and major regions from which 19th-century migrants came:
o: Caribbean islands (Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam), Mauritius, Fiji — Main destinations of Indian indentured migrants
Ceylon and Malaya — Tamil migrants went to work closer to home
Assam tea plantations — Indentured workers were also recruited locally within India
Berlin Conference 1885 — Main destination of Indian indentured peasants to farm wheat in Germany
e: The fourth statement is wrong: the 1885 Berlin Conference was a meeting of European colonial powers to partition Africa, NOT a migration destination for Indian peasants to Germany.

q: Why was the post-World War II Bretton Woods system eventually replaced by a global shift in MNC manufacturing in the late 1970s?
o: Collapse of fixed exchange rates, rise of floating exchange rates, shift of international lending to private Western banks, and relocation of MNC production to low-wage Asian countries like China
Total suspension of air travel worldwide in 1978
Re-imposition of the British Corn Laws in 1980
Return to cowrie shell currency in Asia
e: From the late 1970s, the collapse of Bretton Woods fixed exchange rates, changes in international financial lending, and MNC relocation to low-wage Asian economies reshaped world trade and laid the foundation of modern globalisation.

q: Read this passage from NCERT: "From the 18th century, plantations worked by slaves captured in Africa were growing cotton and sugar for European markets." Who supplied the labour for those 18th-century American plantations, and what replaced them after slavery ended in the 19th century?
o: African slaves in the 18th century; Indian and Chinese indentured labour migration in the 19th century
European aristocrats in the 18th century; American presidents in the 19th century
Japanese samurai in the 18th century; Polish clergy in the 19th century
Australian convicts in both centuries
e: Precious metals from Peru/Mexico enhanced Europe's wealth and financed trade with Asia, while African slaves worked 18th-century cotton/sugar plantations in America; in the 19th century, hundreds of thousands of Indian and Chinese indentured labourers were sent to work on plantations, mines and railways worldwide.

q: Why was the post-World War II "full employment" commitment by Western industrial powers fundamentally different from the laissez-faire policies of the 1920s?
o: Governments realised full employment could not be guaranteed by markets alone and required deliberate state intervention to regulate flows of goods, capital and labour
Governments abolished all factories after 1945
Workers were paid only in silver cowries
No foreign trade was permitted between 1950 and 1970
e: From the inter-war chaos, economists concluded that markets alone cannot guarantee full employment; therefore governments must step in to minimise fluctuations of price, output and employment and control external economic links.

q:
Consider the following statements about indentured labour recruitment:

q: Why did the first Indian indentured migration waves coincide with British abolition of African slavery across the Empire in the 1830s?
o: Plantation owners in Caribbean, Mauritius and Fiji faced acute cheap-labour shortages after emancipation and turned to impoverished Indian and Chinese contract workers
Indian farmers forced plantation owners to hire them at double European wages
Steamships could only carry passengers from Bihar to Fiji
Europe abolished sugar consumption in 1834
e: European colonial plantations and mines urgently needed disciplined cheap labour; combined with rural distress in eastern India and dry Tamil regions, this produced mass indentured migration.

q: Which statement accurately links India's opium trade to China in the 19th century with Britain's tea consumption?
o: British shipments of Indian opium to China generated earnings that Britain used to finance its purchases of tea and other Chinese imports without draining British silver reserves
China paid India directly in potatoes for opium
India imported opium from Britain to brew tea
Britain banned all tea drinking in 1825
e: From the 1820s, opium grown in India was exported in growing quantities to China by the British, and returns from opium sales financed Britain's tea and silk imports from China.

q: What was the long-term impact of refrigerated ships (1870s) not just on nutrition, but also on European domestic politics?
o: Lower meat prices enabled Europe's poor to enjoy better diets (meat, butter, eggs), promoting social peace within European countries and increasing popular support for overseas imperialism
European workers revolted demanding only vegetarian diets
Britain returned all colonies in 1880
Shipping companies went bankrupt globally
e: NCERT specifically notes that better living conditions (affordability of meat, butter and eggs alongside bread and potatoes) promoted social peace within Europe and support for imperialism abroad.

q: Read carefully: "In 1928–1934, India's exports and imports nearly halved, and wheat prices fell by 50%." Yet why did Britain NOT lower land revenue demands in India during the Great Depression?
o: Colonial priorities focused on extracting revenue and maintaining sterling debt/home charges even at the cost of plunging rural Indian peasants into deep debt and forcing distress sales of gold
Because the British government lacked paper to print new tax receipts
Because Indian peasants earned record gold salaries
Because the League of Nations forbade tax cuts in Asia
e: As Keynes observed, colonial policy resulted in Indian gold exports that sped up Britain's economic recovery at the expense of impoverished rural peasants in India.

q:

o: IMF dealt with external surpluses and deficits of member nations, while the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank) was set up to finance post-war reconstruction
IMF financed space rockets while World Bank printed Indian rupees
World Bank dealt solely with 19th-century Corn Laws while IMF funded WWI
Both organisations had identical roles restricted only to Berlin
e: The Bretton Woods Conference established the IMF to deal with external surpluses and deficits of its member nations, and the IBRD (popularly known as the World Bank) to finance post-war reconstruction.

q: What was "food availability" in Europe before and after Columbus's voyages to the Americas?
o: New crops from the Americas — especially the potato — transformed the diets of Europe's poor, enabling them to eat better and live longer
Columbus brought rice from America for the first time to Asia
Before Columbus, Italy already grew tomatoes and chillies natively for 2,000 years
The Americas had zero domesticated crops prior to 1492
e: Foods like potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes and chillies were native to the Americas; after their introduction, Europe's poor began to eat better and live longer with the humble potato.

q: Why does NCERT say "The example of the two world wars" shows that global economic integration can break down dramatically when industrial societies wage total war?
o: Unstable post-war reconstruction, severe European debt to the US, agricultural gluts, trade protectionism, and the collapse of international lending culminating in the 1929 Great Depression
Excessive free trade across Africa
Universal adoption of the $5 wage in every Indian village
Continuous peace and zero inflation from 1914 to 1945
e: Between the two world wars, the pre-war international economic order was shattered by war debts, European agricultural/industrial disruption, protectionist tariffs and the 1929–30s Great Depression until a new framework was designed at Bretton Woods (1944).
